passed.title: cs.string() silently skips Categorical columns
passed.trap: `cs.string` matches only `String` columns by default. Categorical columns are not selected unless you pass `include_categorical=True`. Grouping by `cs.string()` on a frame with a categorical key therefore drops that key without any error, and the aggregates merge groups that should stay separate. Use `cs.string(include_categorical=True)`, or combine selectors with `cs.string() | cs.categorical()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"w": ["a", "a", "b"], "z": ["x", "y", "x"], "v": [1, 2, 4]}
).with_columns(pl.col("z").cast(pl.Categorical))

# WRONG: 'z' is not used as a key, so a/x and a/y collapse into one group
wrong = df.group_by(cs.string()).agg(cs.numeric().sum()).sort("w")
print(wrong.columns, wrong["v"].to_list())

# RIGHT: include categorical keys explicitly
right = (
    df.group_by(cs.string(include_categorical=True))
    .agg(cs.numeric().sum())
    .sort("v")
)
print(right.columns, right["v"].to_list())

passed.title: Use cs.matches for regex; contains/starts_with/ends_with are literal
passed.trap: `cs.contains`, `cs.starts_with` and `cs.ends_with` match literal substrings, so `"."` means a real dot. `cs.matches` takes a regex and is not anchored: it selects any column whose name contains a match anywhere. A bare `cs.matches(".")` therefore selects every column. Add `^` and `$` (and escape metacharacters) when you want an exact pattern.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"a.b": [1], "axb": [2], "total_a": [3]})

print(df.select(cs.contains(".")).columns)       # literal dot
print(df.select(cs.matches(".")).columns)        # regex: any char -> all
print(df.select(cs.matches("a")).columns)        # unanchored search
print(df.select(cs.matches("^a")).columns)       # anchored at start
print(df.select(cs.matches(r"^a\.b$")).columns)  # exact, escaped

passed.title: cs.alpha and cs.alphanumeric reject underscores and accept Unicode
passed.trap: `cs.alphanumeric` and `cs.alpha` require every character of the name to be a letter (or a digit, for alphanumeric). Snake_case names such as `user_id` are excluded. By default they also accept the full Unicode range, so `café` matches. Pass `ascii_only=True` to restrict to ASCII. For identifier-like names, use an explicit `cs.matches` pattern instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"user_id": [1], "score": [2], "q1": [3], "café": [4]})

print(df.select(cs.alphanumeric()).columns)  # user_id excluded
print(df.select(cs.alphanumeric(ascii_only=True)).columns)
print(df.select(cs.alpha()).columns)
# Explicit ASCII identifier pattern, underscores allowed
print(df.select(cs.matches(r"^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$")).columns)

passed.title: cs.datetime(time_zone=None) means naive only, not any zone
passed.trap: The default `time_zone` of `cs.datetime` is `('*', None)`, which matches both tz-aware and naive columns. Passing `time_zone=None` does not mean "don't filter": it selects only columns without a timezone. `"*"` selects only tz-aware columns. `time_unit` is also a filter, so `cs.datetime("ms")` selects nothing when the columns use the default `us` unit.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"naive": [datetime(2024, 1, 1)]}).with_columns(
    utc=pl.col("naive").dt.replace_time_zone("UTC")
)

print(df.select(cs.datetime()).columns)                 # both
print(df.select(cs.datetime(time_zone=None)).columns)   # naive only
print(df.select(cs.datetime(time_zone="*")).columns)    # tz-aware only
print(df.select(cs.datetime("ms")).columns)             # [] (columns are us)

passed.title: cs.first and cs.last pick columns, not rows
passed.trap: `cs.first` and `cs.last` select the first or last column of the current scope. They do not return the first or last value of a column. For values, use `Expr.first` or `Expr.last` on an expression, for example `pl.all().first()`. Because the selection is positional, adding a column with `DataFrame.with_columns` changes what `cs.last()` refers to.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["b", "a"], "v": [10, 20]})

print(df.select(cs.first()))         # whole 'name' column, 2 rows
print(df.select(pl.all().first()))   # first row of every column

print(df.select(cs.last()).columns)  # ['v']
df2 = df.with_columns(v2=pl.col("v") * 2)
print(df2.select(cs.last()).columns) # now ['v2']

passed.title: cs.by_name and cs.by_index raise on missing columns and reorder output
passed.trap: `cs.by_name` and `cs.by_index` default to `require_all=True`. One missing name or out-of-bounds index raises an error instead of being skipped. Pass `require_all=False` to keep only the columns that exist. Both selectors return columns in the order you list them, not in schema order, so do not assume the output keeps the frame's column order.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2], "c": [3]})

try:
    df.select(cs.by_name("c", "missing"))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

print(df.select(cs.by_name("c", "missing", require_all=False)).columns)
# Order follows the selector, not the schema
print(df.select(cs.by_name("c", "a")).columns)
print(df.select(cs.by_index(-1, 0)).columns)

passed.title: cs.exclude silently ignores names that do not exist
passed.trap: `cs.exclude` accepts names, dtypes and selectors. A name that matches no column is ignored without an error. A typo or a wrong-case name therefore leaves the column you meant to remove in the result. When the column must exist, use `DataFrame.drop`, which errors on unknown names by default.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "price": [9.5, 3.0], "qty": [2, 4]})

# WRONG: typo 'ID' is silently ignored, so 'id' is still there
print(df.select(cs.exclude("ID")).columns)

# RIGHT: DataFrame.drop fails loudly on the typo
try:
    df.drop("ID")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
print(df.drop("id").columns)

passed.title: cs.expand_selector is strict and rejects plain expressions
passed.trap: `cs.expand_selector` defaults to `strict=True` and only expands genuine selectors. A plain column expression such as `pl.col(...)` is not a selector (`cs.is_selector` returns False), so in strict mode it fails. Pass `strict=False` to expand broader column expressions. Alternatively, build the selection from selectors only, for example with set difference (`cs.numeric() - cs.by_name("id")`).
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1], "x": [1.0], "s": ["a"]})

print(cs.is_selector(pl.col("id")), cs.is_selector(cs.numeric()))
print(cs.expand_selector(df, cs.numeric() - cs.by_name("id")))

try:
    cs.expand_selector(df, pl.col("id", "s"))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

print(cs.expand_selector(df, pl.col("id", "s"), strict=False))
